statement: The supplied sources do not contain a derivation of integration by parts (noting only that it is an integral version of the product rule of differentiation and is derived using the product rule). As defined and formulated in the sources, the integration by parts formula states: \int u \, dv = u \cdot v - \int v \, du (or \int u \, dv = uv - \int v \, du).

symbols.meaning: function or factor chosen to be differentiated
differential factor chosen to be integrated

properties.why: finds the integral of a product of functions in terms of the integral of the product of their derivative and antiderivative to transform it into a more easily solved form
is derived directly using the product rule of differentiation
repeated applications of the formula to integrals of the form \int x^n e^x dx, \int x^n \sin(x) dx, or \int x^n \cos(x) dx lower the power of x by one per application

properties.property: Integration of functions multiplied by unity
properties.why: evaluates functions like \ln(x) or \arctan(x) by writing them as a product with 1 when the derivative is known and the integral of the derivative times x is known

properties.property: Cyclic integral evaluation via algebraic rearrangement
properties.why: solves integrals like \int e^x \cos(x) dx where the original integral reappears with opposite sign after repeated application, allowing it to be solved by adding the integral to both sides
yields recursive functional relationships such as the Gamma function identity \Gamma(z) = (z-1)\Gamma(z-1) and the Wallis product for \pi

assumptions.assumption: The integrand can be factored into parts u and dv such that du is simpler than u and dv is easy to integrate
assumptions.breaks_when: No choice of factor dv has an elementary or accessible antiderivative

assumptions.assumption: When integrating a function multiplied by 1, the derivative of the function is known and the integral of this derivative multiplied by x is also known
assumptions.breaks_when: The product of x and the derivative of the function does not possess a known antiderivative

failure_modes.signature: Application yields an integral with higher powers or greater complexity (e.g., choosing u = \cos(x) and dv = x\,dx yields \int \frac{x^2}{2}\sin(x)\,dx)
failure_modes.cause: Suboptimal choice of u and dv contrary to heuristic selection guidelines such as LIATE/ILATE

failure_modes.mode: Failure of naive factor selection under LIATE
failure_modes.signature: Directly assigning u based solely on LIATE order leaves a factor dv that cannot be integrated
failure_modes.cause: Integrands with composite arguments (e.g., \int x^3 e^{x^2}\,dx) require non-trivial splitting of polynomial terms (such as setting u = x^2 and dv = x e^{x^2}\,dx)

canon_notes: canon expects a derivation but no source performs one, so integration_by_parts is recorded as a definition
